# scriptc: TypeScript-to-Native Compiler

**What it is:** scriptc is a compiler that transforms TypeScript code into native binaries without requiring Node.js, V8, or a JavaScript engine embedded in the output.

**Language & Runtime:** It's a TypeScript compiler (not a runtime) created by Vercel Labs. The source language is standard TypeScript, compiled to native machine code.

**Relationship to JavaScript/TypeScript:** scriptc accepts "ordinary TypeScript" and uses the real TypeScript compiler for type-checking. It's designed to work with code you'd normally run on Node.js, but produces standalone native executables instead.

**Supported Features:** The documentation indicates support for:
- Classes, closures, and async/await
- Standard library features
- Node.js APIs (fs, path, process, http surfaces)

**Unsupported/Dynamic Features:** Code that can't compile statically (like npm dependencies' shipped JavaScript or untyped code) requires opting into a dynamic tier with an embedded ~620KB JavaScript engine. Everything else "fails the build with a specific error code" rather than silently miscompiling.

**How Code Runs:** There are three tiers: static compilation by default, optional dynamic execution with an embedded JS engine, and compile-time rejection of unsupported constructs.

**Maturity & Creator:** The project has 4.5k GitHub stars and supports macOS, Linux, and Windows. It's maintained by Vercel Labs. The documentation emphasizes differential testing against Node.js for correctness validation.

Short answer: **not in any way that would matter.** I dug into it — scriptc (Vercel Labs) compiles TypeScript to native binaries with no JS engine, and its static tier achieves that by removing exactly the dynamism ivue is built on.

The disqualifiers from their own docs, mapped to our engine:

- **Records are structs, not objects.** `Object.keys` reports *declaration* order, shapes are exact (`{a,b}` into `{a}` fails the build), and — the killer — "structural width subtyping **copies**, not aliases; mutations through narrower references are invisible to the original." Reactivity is aliasing-or-nothing: if flowing a value into a function copies it, every ref, every proxy, every subscription breaks. This alone rules out Vue itself, before ivue enters the picture.
- **No runtime metaprogramming.** `Reactive()` is a subclass factory that walks `getOwnPropertyDescriptors` and rewrites the prototype with `defineProperty` at runtime; cells materialize as own properties on first touch; methods bind lazily. In a static tier where objects are compiled structs, there *is no prototype to rewrite* — this isn't a missing feature, it's the definition of their model.
- **Vue's substrate** is `Proxy` + `WeakMap` + `Symbol`-keyed internals; their limitations page fences `Symbol`, restricts Map/Set keys to strings and numbers, and rejects `globalThis`.

There's a **dynamic tier** (`--dynamic`) that embeds a ~620KB JS engine for "npm dependencies' shipped JS" — ivue+Vue would presumably *run* there. But then you're just executing JavaScript in a small embedded interpreter instead of V8: you keep none of scriptc's native-speed benefit and lose most of the engine performance our benchmarks are measured on. Technically alive, practically pointless.

The interesting part is the philosophy: scriptc and ivue are **opposite bets on the same fact**. `what-javascript-becomes` argues the runtime's dynamism is the *asset* — lazy linking, hot-swappable classes, cells that exist only when touched, all as userland conventions. scriptc bets that dynamism is the *tax*, and pays for native output by freezing objects into structs at compile time. Both are coherent; they just can't host each other. If TS-to-native matures, the ivue-shaped question for that world wouldn't be "port the engine" but "what does lazy existence look like when the compiler owns layout" — which is the same question the TC39-signals article poses to engines, one level down.

So: static tier — structurally impossible by design; dynamic tier — runs but defeats both tools' purposes. ivue's native-adjacent story remains Bun/Node (the backend guide's lane) and, longer-term, native signal slots in real engines.

# Blog comments — design, mechanics, invariants

The complete description of the threaded comments system as shipped on
2026-08-24. Read this before touching `newsletter/src/modules/comments/`,
`newsletter/src/modules/api/PublicApi.ts` (comment routes),
`newsletter/src/modules/api/AdminApi.ts` (moderation routes),
`newsletter/src/modules/delivery/Delivery.ts` (`notifyReply`),
`newsletter/src/modules/platform/Security.ts` (thread/avatar tokens),
`docs_v2/.vitepress/theme/components/BlogComments.vue`,
`CommentAvatar.vue`, or the dashboard's `comments/` module.

The last section lists the invariants explicitly and the known gaps
where the current code does NOT yet enforce one. That section is the
starting point for the invariants work.

---

## 1. Data model (D1)

Migrations `0008_comments.sql` + `0009_comment_threads.sql`.

```
comments
  id            INTEGER PK AUTOINCREMENT
  slug          TEXT      -- the post; validated /^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$/
  name          TEXT      -- display name, ≤ 80 chars, trimmed
  email         TEXT      -- lowercased; OPERATOR-ONLY, never served publicly
  body          TEXT      -- plain text, ≤ 2000 chars
  submitted_at  INTEGER   -- unix seconds
  status        TEXT      -- 'pending' | 'approved'   (default 'pending')
  parent_id     INTEGER   -- NULL for a top-level comment; else the
                          -- comment being ANSWERED (root or a reply)
  root_id       INTEGER   -- the thread: = own id for a top-level comment,
                          -- = the root's id for every reply (any depth)
  locked        INTEGER   -- 0/1, meaningful ONLY on the root row
  avatar_seed   TEXT      -- 16 hex chars; HMAC(ADMIN_SECRET, 'avatar:'+email)
                          -- (plain SHA-256 prefix when no secret — local dev)

comment_subscriptions
  root_id       INTEGER   -- the thread followed
  email         TEXT      -- lowercased
  created_at    INTEGER
  PRIMARY KEY (root_id, email)

indexes: comments(slug, status), comments(root_id, submitted_at)
```

Shape rules:

- **Depth is exactly two.** A row is either a root (`parent_id NULL`,
  `root_id = id`) or a reply (`parent_id` set, `root_id` = its root).
  A reply to a reply has `parent_id` = the reply it answers but the
  SAME `root_id` — the tree never grows a third level. "Who it
  answers" and "which thread it's in" are separate columns on purpose.
- `locked` is read only from the root row. `setLocked(id)` resolves
  `rootId` first, so locking via a reply's id locks its thread.
- `avatar_seed` is the commenter's public identity handle. Same email →
  same seed everywhere; the email is not derivable from it.

## 2. Lifecycle of a comment

```
submit (POST /comment)          → row INSERTed as 'pending'
                                → root: UPDATE root_id = id
                                → reply subscription INSERTed (if opted in)
                                → operator notified (NOTIFY_EMAIL)
                                → NOTHING is public yet
approve (POST /admin/comments/approve)
                                → status = 'approved' (the ONLY path to public)
                                → if it is a reply: reply notifications go out NOW
delete (POST /admin/comments/delete)
                                → DELETE that one row (see gap G1)
lock/unlock (POST /admin/comments/lock)
                                → root.locked = 0/1
```

1. slug shape, name present, email pattern, body present, body ≤ 2000.
2. If `parentId` given: parent must exist, be **approved** (you cannot
   reply into an invisible comment), be on the **same slug**, and its
   thread must be **unlocked**. Reader-facing errors: "That comment is
   no longer available." / "That comment belongs to another post." /
   "Replies are locked on this thread."
3. `avatar_seed` computed from the email.
4. INSERT as pending; for a root, second statement sets `root_id = id`.
5. If `subscribeReplies !== false` (default TRUE —

## 9. Known gaps / open questions (input to the invariants work)

- **G1 — Orphaned replies on delete.** `remove(id)` deletes ONE row.
  Deleting a root leaves replies with `root_id`/`parent_id` pointing at
  nothing: they vanish from the site (client only renders replies
  under a rendered root) but remain in D1, still notify-eligible, and
  the dashboard shows "reply in thread #N" for a missing N. Options:
  cascade delete; or "tombstone" the root (keep row, blank body, mark
  deleted) so replies survive with "[deleted]"; or re-parent. Decide,
  then make I8 real.
- **G2 — Subscription before approval.** See I21. Options: create the
  subscription at approval time instead (requires remembering the
  opt-in — add a column), or keep and document.
- **G3 — Name is not identity.** Anyone can post as "Ada". The avatar
  seed (from email) is the real identity signal — two "Ada"s get
  different identicons — but @mention matching is by NAME, so a
  mention can resolve to an impostor's row and notify the impostor
  (only if they follow the thread). Consider matching mentions to
  avatar_seed/email of the *earliest* participant with that name, or
  rendering `@Name` with the identicon, or disallowing duplicate
  display names within a thread.
- **G4 — No rate limiting** beyond Turnstile. Pending-by-default means
  spam has no payoff, but D1 rows accumulate.
- **G5 — Body length only; no link/markdown policy.** Plain text is
  interpolated; URLs are not linkified. Fine, but implicit.
- **G6 — Thread tokens never expire.** Acceptable for unsubscribe

- **G7 — `locked` on a non-root row is ignored but possible** if

- **G8 — Approve is idempotent for notifications by SQL accident**

your opinion on posts vs blogs vs newsletters

My honest take: **"posts" is the correct word, and "blogs" is the one I'd avoid.**

**What each word actually names**

- **Blog** = the publication, singular. `/blog/` is *the* blog. Each entry in it is a **post**. "Blogs" (plural) reads as *multiple publications* — "I read a few blogs" means a few different sites. So "All blogs" and "Search blogs…" literally promise a list of websites, and a first-time reader has to do a small correction in their head. It's a common casual usage, but it's the one that reads as slightly off to native-English developers, and your standard is first-time-reader clarity.
- **Newsletter** = a *delivery channel*, not the content. The same words arrive as a web page or as an email. Calling the sidebar "Newsletters" labels the archive by one of its two channels, and it's the channel the reader on the website is *not* using — they're reading the web, not their inbox. It also collides with the signup CTA: "Get the blog as a newsletter" only makes sense if the blog and the newsletter are different things. If the list is already "Newsletters," what are they getting?
- **Post** = the unit. Unambiguous, matches your own code (`posts`, `BlogPostNav`, `relatedPosts`), matches the "46 posts" counter still on the index heading, and matches how every dev reader already thinks about it.

**Consistency check on the current state**

Right now the same page says "Blog" (h1), "46 posts" (counter), "Search blogs…" (search), "All blogs" (rail), and "Blogs" (sub-nav) — three names for the unit, on one screen. That's exactly the "one concept, one name" failure the write-docs skill warns about, just in UI copy.

**What I'd ship**

- Sub-nav button: **Blog** (it names the section, like Guide / Examples / Releases — those are section names, not units; "Guide" isn't "Guides").
- Rail head: **All posts**
- Both search boxes: **Search posts…**
- Keep "Get the blog as a newsletter" — it's the one place "newsletter" belongs, because it's describing the channel.

If your instinct behind "blogs" is that "posts" feels generic or social-media-ish — that's fair, but "articles" solves that cleanly ("All articles", "Search articles…") without the plural-publication problem. Between the two I'd still pick posts for consistency with the counter and codebase, but articles is a defensible second.

Your call — say the word and I'll set whichever you choose everywhere in one commit.

**Keep "Blog."** Two reasons, both about what the button *is*:

1. **It names a section, not the unit.** Its siblings are Guide / Examples / Releases — section names. And it would break the parallel with the top nav, which already says **Blog** — the mobile sub-nav button opening the blog's sidebar should say the same word the reader tapped to get there.

"Articles → All articles → Search articles…" says the same word three times and loses the section/unit distinction that makes "All articles" meaningful.
